usage: By far the most common sport to open small talk with Korean coworkers and friends.
Let's play a round of soccer
판 is the casual counter for a round/match; 한 판 하다 = 'play a round', breezier than 경기.
Want to go watch a soccer game?
보러 가다 = 'go in order to watch'; the 러 attaches to the verb stem of the purpose.
조기(早起, 'rising early') 축구 is a fixed term for the weekend dawn matches older men famously play.
examples: 주말마다 친구들이랑 축구 해요.
I play soccer with my friends every weekend.
마다 = 'every'; in speech 축구(를) 하다 drops the 를, and 이랑 is the casual 'with'.
어젯밤에 손흥민 나오는 축구 경기 봤어요?
Did you watch the soccer match Son Heung-min was in last night?
나오다 = 'appear/be featured'; EPL games with 손흥민 are huge water-cooler talk.
한국이 일본을 이겨서 축구 팬들이 다 난리 났어요.
Korea beat Japan, so all the soccer fans went wild.
난리 나다 = 'go into an uproar'; -아서 here marks the cause leading to the reaction.
nuance: 축구 (蹴球, literally 'kick(蹴)-ball(球)') is the default national sport for casual conversation, and dropping a name like 손흥민 buys instant rapport, especially in men's chat. The verb splits by activity: 축구(를) 하다 for playing versus 축구(를) 보다 for watching — never one verb for both, and in speech the 를 is usually dropped. The big English-speaker pitfall is the word itself: do NOT say 풋볼, which Koreans hear as American football, nor 사커; the only natural word is 축구. A second trap is calling a real match 축구 게임 — for a broadcast or pro fixture it is 축구 경기, while 게임 sounds like a casual pickup kickabout. Recognize the cultural compound 조기 축구, the dawn amateur soccer older men play on weekends.

Saying 축구를 보다 and 축구를 하다 interchangeably — you watch (보다) a match but play (하다) the sport; the verbs are not swappable.

usage: Korea's most-attended pro sport (KBO); a safe, friendly small-talk opener.
Which team do you root for?
응원하다 = 'cheer for'; asking someone's KBO team is a classic bonding move.
Let's go to a baseball game
보러 가다 again; KBO stadiums are famous for loud, organized fan chants.
시즌 is the everyday loanword; the KBO season runs spring through fall.
examples: 주말에 잠실 가서 야구 볼 거예요.
I'm going to Jamsil this weekend to watch baseball.
Locals name the venue: 잠실 가다 rather than 야구장 가다; -ㄹ 거예요 = future plan.
야구장 가면 치킨에 맥주는 필수예요.
When you go to a baseball stadium, chicken and beer are a must.
치킨에 맥주 = 'chicken plus beer' (the 에 means 'added to'); 필수 = 'a must'.
우리 팀이 9회에 역전해서 진짜 짜릿했어요.
Our team came from behind in the 9th, it was such a thrill.
역전(逆轉)하다 = 'reverse the lead'; 9회 = the 9th inning, 에 marks the time point.
nuance: 야구 (野球, literally 'field(野)-ball(球)') is arguably the sport Koreans are most passionate about attending in person — the stadium chants, team songs, and bringing your own 치맥 (치킨+맥주) form a whole culture. The verb pattern mirrors 축구: 야구(를) 하다 for playing, 야구(를) 보다 for watching. Asking 어느 팀 응원해요? signals you want to connect socially. Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, for a pro game Koreans usually name the stadium (잠실 가다, 고척 가다) — saying 야구장 가다 sounds like a generic or amateur field. Second, 회 here is the inning counter (1회, 9회), a homophone of 회 'raw fish'; the number and context disambiguate, so 9회 unambiguously means the ninth inning, never sashimi.

usage: Do you know how to play basketball?
할 줄 알다 = 'know how to do'; the natural way to propose a pickup game.
Let's play a game of basketball
게임 works for pickup hoops; 한 게임 = 'one game', unlike pro soccer where you'd want 경기.
골대 = the hoop/goal post; you'll see them at parks and schoolyards.
Many younger Koreans follow the NBA; the acronym is spelled out in English letters.
examples: 퇴근하고 동료들이랑 농구 하러 가요.
After work I go play basketball with coworkers.
하러 가다 = 'go in order to play'; 퇴근하고 = 'after clocking out'.
키 크면 농구 잘할 것 같다는 말 많이 들어요.
People often tell me I'd be good at basketball since I'm tall.
잘하다 = 'be good at'; -다는 말 듣다 = 'hear people say that...'.
동네 농구장에서 모르는 사람들이랑 게임했어요.
I played a game with strangers at the neighborhood court.
농구장 = 'basketball court'; pickup games (픽업 게임) with strangers are common.
nuance: 농구 (籠球, literally 'basket(籠)-ball(球)') had a huge cultural moment in the 90s through the drama '마지막 승부' and the 'Slam Dunk' generation, and pickup games at neighborhood 농구장 remain popular among younger men. The verb is 농구(를) 하다 for playing, 농구(를) 보다 for watching. A useful register note for English speakers: unlike pro soccer, with basketball you can freely say 농구 게임 for a casual pickup game (한 게임 하자), though 농구 경기 is still the word for a formal or broadcast match — so 게임 here is not a mistake the way it would be for a pro 축구 fixture. The two pitfalls are the loanword 바스켓볼 (never used; only 농구) and calling the hoop 농구 문 ('basketball door') instead of the correct 골대.

Saying 농구 문 ('basketball door') for the hoop; the correct word is 골대 (or 농구 골대).
Forcing 경기 onto every casual game — for pickup hoops, 농구 한 게임 하자 is perfectly natural, unlike with pro soccer.

usage: Women's pro volleyball (V-리그) has a strong, growing fanbase in Korea.
Did you watch the volleyball match?
경기 is the standard word for a formal match in any sport.
국가대표(國家代表) = 'national team', often heard around 김연경 and the Olympics.
배구 was a staple P.E. and 체육대회 (sports day) game for many Koreans.
examples: 김연경 선수 덕분에 배구 팬이 많아졌어요.
Thanks to Kim Yeon-koung, volleyball gained a lot of fans.
덕분에 = 'thanks to' (positive cause only); 선수 = 'athlete', a respectful tag after a name.
우리 회사 체육대회 때 배구 시합 했어요.
We had a volleyball match at our company sports day.
시합 = match/contest, interchangeable with 경기 in casual use; 때 = 'at the time of'.
배구는 키가 큰 선수들이 유리한 것 같아요.
It seems taller players have an advantage in volleyball.
유리하다 = 'be advantageous'; -ㄴ 것 같다 softens it to 'it seems'.
nuance: 배구 (排球, literally 'push/arrange(排)-ball(球)', capturing how the ball is set and pushed over the net) surged in popularity through women's pro volleyball and especially 김연경 (Kim Yeon-koung), making it a warmer small-talk topic than before. It is also a nostalgic schoolyard and company sports-day (체육대회) game. For a match you can use 경기 or the slightly more casual, contest-flavored 시합 (試合) — the dividing line is that 시합 emphasizes the head-to-head contest while 경기 is the neutral all-purpose term. The pitfall for English speakers is the loanword 발리볼, which sounds foreign and is never used; say 배구. Also note 배구 is a clear two-syllable word, so it never gets confused in practice with the bare 배 (boat/stomach/pear).

Assuming 시합 and 경기 are different things — they overlap heavily; 시합 just leans toward 'contest/bout' while 경기 is neutral.
Dropping a syllable to 배 — the sport is always the full 배구; 배 alone means boat/stomach/pear.

usage: Note the verb: 탁구는 치다 ('hit'), not 하다 — like other paddle/racket sports.
Shall we play a round of ping-pong?
치다 + 판; -ㄹ까요 makes it a soft 'shall we?' suggestion at a community center.
Dedicated 탁구장 are common in neighborhoods and apartment complexes.
The paddle is 라켓; the table itself is 탁구대.
examples: 점심시간에 회사 휴게실에서 탁구 쳐요.
During lunch we play ping-pong in the office lounge.
휴게실 = 'break room'; note 탁구 쳐요 (from 치다), and 에서 marks the location of the action.
탁구는 운동도 되고 재미도 있어서 좋아요.
Table tennis is good because it's both exercise and fun.
운동이 되다 = 'count as exercise'; -도...-도 = 'both...and'.
아파트 주민센터에 탁구대가 있어서 자주 쳐요.
There's a table tennis table at the apartment center, so I play often.
있어서 = 'there is, so'; the object 탁구 is dropped before 쳐요 because it's understood.
nuance: 탁구 (卓球, literally 'table(卓)-ball(球)') is crucial for one reason English speakers stumble on: it takes the verb 치다 ('to hit/strike'), NOT 하다 — you say 탁구를 치다. This 치다 is the same verb used for hitting a ball with an implement (tennis, golf, drums), the dividing line from 하다, which is for sports you do with your whole body or feet (축구를 하다). It is an accessible, low-cost way to socialize, found in 탁구장, apartment community rooms, and office break rooms. Vocabulary to keep straight: the table is 탁구대 and the paddle is 라켓. A register pitfall: calling it 핑퐁 in conversation sounds childish or cutesy; adults say 탁구.

The verb is the thing English speakers stumble on: it is 치다, not 하다. A register pitfall: calling it 핑퐁 in conversation sounds childish or cutesy; adults say 탁구.

mistakes: Saying 탁구 하다 instead of the natural 탁구 치다 — paddle sports take 치다.
Calling it 핑퐁 in adult conversation — that sounds childish; say 탁구.
Mixing up 탁구대 (the table) and 라켓 (the paddle) — they are different pieces of equipment.

usage: Like table tennis, tennis takes 치다 (to hit), not 하다.
-고 있다 = ongoing; 테니스 has boomed as a trendy lesson-based hobby for 20-30s.
예약하다 = 'reserve'; public 테니스장 fill up fast and are booked by app.
레슨 is the standard word; beginners often start with a 강습/레슨 package.
examples: 요즘 테니스 배우는 사람 진짜 많아졌어요.
These days way more people are learning tennis.
많아지다 = 'become many/increase'; 요즘 sets the recent-trend frame.
주말에 테니스장 잡기가 하늘의 별 따기예요.
Booking a court on weekends is like picking a star from the sky.
하늘의 별 따기 = idiom for 'nearly impossible'; 잡다 here = 'secure/book'.
테니스 치고 나면 온몸이 다 쑤셔요.
After playing tennis my whole body aches.
-고 나면 = 'after (completing)'; 온몸이 쑤시다 = 'whole body aches'.
nuance: 테니스 is a loanword (no hanja), and the key thing English speakers get wrong is the verb: it is 치다 ('to hit'), exactly like 탁구 and 골프, because you strike a ball with a racket — never 테니스를 하다. In recent years it has become a fashionable lifestyle hobby for Koreans in their 20s-30s, complete with 테니스 룩 (tennis outfits) for social media, so the word now signals a trendy, active social circle. Court booking (테니스장 예약) is genuinely competitive on weekends. One vocabulary contrast worth knowing: the older term 정구 refers specifically to soft tennis and sounds dated, so for the modern racket sport always say 테니스.

Translating 'book a court' word-for-word — Koreans say 테니스장 예약하다, with 예약 ('reservation'), not a literal rendering of 'book'.

usage: Golf also takes 치다; a common question among professionals and older colleagues.
스크린 골프 (indoor simulator golf) is hugely popular and affordable in Korea.
I'm in the middle of learning golf
-는 중이다 = 'in the process of'; golf lessons have spread to younger people.
골프장 = the course; 'going out to the course' = 필드 나가다.
examples: 주말에 친구들이랑 스크린 골프 치러 갔어요.
On the weekend I went to play screen golf with friends.
치러 가다 = 'go in order to play (hit)'; 스크린 골프 is social and often paired with drinks.
골프는 장비값이 비싸서 시작하기 부담돼요.
Golf is daunting to start because the equipment is expensive.
부담되다 = 'feel burdensome'; -기 turns 시작하다 into the noun 'starting'.
부장님이 주말마다 골프 치러 필드 나가세요.
My boss goes out to the course to play golf every weekend.
필드 나가다 = 'go out to the real course'; -세요 is the honorific for the senior 부장님.
nuance: 골프 is a loanword (no hanja), and like the other racket/club sports it takes 치다 ('to hit') — 골프를 치다, never 골프를 하다, because you strike the ball with a club. Socially it carries a slightly upscale, business-networking image, but 스크린 골프 (screen/simulator golf) has made it casual and accessible — a common night out with friends and coworkers. Two insider words English speakers should learn: the real outdoor course is called 필드 ('field'), and 필드 나가다 means 'go play on an actual course' (as opposed to the screen). In casual speech, plain 골프 치러 가자 often actually means 스크린 골프, so don't assume every mention implies an expensive outdoor round.

Not knowing 필드 — Koreans call the real course 필드 and say 필드 나가다 for playing outdoors; 골프장 is the formal term.

usage: Do you know how to ski?
Crucial verb: 스키는 타다 ('ride'), used for gear you stand on and ride.
타러 가다 = 'go in order to ride/do'; winter resort trips are common.
스키장 covers the whole resort; the major ones are in 강원도.
빌리다 = 'borrow/rent'; renting (대여) gear at the resort is normal for casual skiers.
examples: 겨울에 강원도로 스키 타러 갈 거예요.
This winter I'm going to Gangwon-do to ski.
-로 marks direction toward 강원도; 타러 가다 = 'go to ski'.
스키는 처음이라 초보자 코스에서 탔어요.
It was my first time skiing, so I rode the beginner course.
처음이라 = 'since it's the first time'; 초보자 코스 = 'beginner course'.
스키 탈 때 넘어지면 진짜 아파요.
When you fall while skiing, it really hurts.
넘어지다 = 'fall down'; -ㄹ 때 = 'when/while doing'.
nuance: 스키 is a loanword (no hanja), and the verb is the whole lesson here: it takes 타다 ('to ride'), never 하다 — 스키를 타다. 타다 is the verb for anything you mount, board, or stand on to move (bus, bike, ski, skateboard), which is exactly why ski, snowboard, and skates all use it rather than 하다. Winter ski trips to 강원도 resorts are a popular group outing, often combined with 보드 (snowboarding) at the same place. The resort and slopes together are 스키장, and gear rental (대여/빌리다) is the norm for casual participants. The pitfall, besides 스키 하다, is conflating 스키 with 보드/스노보드 — they are different activities done at the same 스키장.

Using 하다 for board sports too — snowboarding is also 보드(를) 타다, not 하다.

usage: Like 스키, skating takes 타다, since you stand on the blades and ride.
타러 가자 = casual 'let's go to skate'; a popular winter date activity.
스케이트장 = the ice rink; seasonal outdoor rinks pop up in winter.
스케이트화 = the boots themselves (화 = 'footwear'); rented at the rink.
examples: 겨울에 야외 스케이트장에서 스케이트 탔어요.
In winter I went skating at an outdoor rink.
야외 = 'outdoor'; seasonal rinks at city plazas are popular dates.
스케이트 처음 타는 사람은 벽 잡고 타요.
First-timers skate while holding onto the wall.
벽 잡고 = 'gripping the wall'; -고 links the two simultaneous actions.
김연아 덕분에 피겨 스케이트 인기가 많아졌어요.
Thanks to Kim Yu-na, figure skating became very popular.
피겨 스케이트 = 'figure skating'; 덕분에 marks the positive cause.
nuance: 스케이트 is a loanword (no hanja) and, like 스키, takes 타다 ('to ride') — 스케이트를 타다 — because you stand on the blades and glide; 하다 is wrong. Korea has a strong skating culture thanks to short-track and figure stars like 김연아 (Kim Yu-na), and seasonal outdoor 스케이트장 are a classic winter date spot. The vocabulary to keep distinct trips up English speakers: 스케이트장 is the rink (place), while 스케이트화 is the boots (화 = footwear), and bare 스케이트 can mean the activity or loosely the gear. Also distinguish ice 스케이트 from 인라인/롤러 (inline/roller skating), which likewise take 타다 but happen on wheels, not ice.

usage: Marathons take the verb 뛰다 (to run); 달리다 also works.
대회(大會) = 'tournament/event'; weekend city marathons are common.
하프(half) 마라톤 — many beginners start here before a 풀코스 (full course).
I signed up for a marathon
신청하다 = 'apply/register'; entries open online and fill up fast.
examples: 이번 가을에 처음으로 하프 마라톤 뛰어요.
This fall I'm running my first half marathon.
처음으로 = 'for the first time'; the present tense here states a fixed near plan.
마라톤 완주하면 메달 줘요.
If you finish the marathon, they give you a medal.
완주(完走)하다 = 'run the full course'; -면 = 'if/when', 줘요 has an unstated 'they'.
요즘 러닝이 유행이라 마라톤 대회마다 사람이 많아요.
Running is trendy lately, so every marathon event is packed.
유행이라 = 'since it's a trend'; 마다 = 'every (single)'.
nuance: 마라톤 is a loanword (no hanja) and fits the current 러닝 (running) boom among Koreans in their 20s-30s, where running crews and weekend 마라톤 대회 are genuinely trendy social scenes. The verb is 뛰다 or 달리다 ('to run') — not 하다; the fine distinction is that 뛰다 is the everyday word that also means 'jump/sprint', while 달리다 is a touch more squarely 'run/dash', and for marathons the two are interchangeable. Useful related words: 완주 (完走, 'complete the run') means finishing the full distance, and many start with a 하프 마라톤 before attempting the 풀코스. The pitfall for English speakers is assuming 마라톤 always means the full 42.195km; in casual use it loosely covers any race distance run at a 마라톤 대회.

usage: 경기 is the standard word for a sports match in any sport.
시작하다 = 'begin'; said the moment a match kicks off.
결과(結果) = 'result'; 경기 결과 is how you ask the final score/outcome.
있다 = 'there is'; a common check before planning to watch.
examples: 오늘 저녁에 중요한 축구 경기가 있어요.
There's an important soccer match this evening.
Attach 경기 after the sport: 축구 경기, 야구 경기; 이/가 있다 = 'there is'.
경기가 너무 박빙이라 끝까지 손에 땀을 쥐었어요.
The game was so close I was on edge until the end.
박빙 = 'neck and neck'; 손에 땀을 쥐다 = idiom 'be on the edge of your seat'.
비 와서 오늘 경기는 취소됐어요.
The game was canceled today because of rain.
취소되다 = 'be canceled' (passive); 비 와서 = 'because it rained'.
nuance: 경기 (競技, literally 'compete(競)-skill(技)', i.e. a contest of skill) is the all-purpose word for a sporting match and pairs with any sport (축구 경기, 야구 경기). The key contrast for English speakers is register: 경기 is the neutral, formal-friendly term for pro and broadcast sports, whereas the loanword 게임 fits casual pickup play — so defaulting to 게임 for a real match sounds off. A close synonym is 시합 (試合), which leans slightly toward 'contest/bout' and is common in spoken, head-to-head contexts; 경기 stays the safe neutral choice. The classic trap is the homophone: 경기 also means 'the economy' (경기가 안 좋다 = 'the economy is bad'), an unrelated word with different hanja (景氣) — only context tells them apart, but in a sports conversation 경기 is always the match.

mistakes: Defaulting to 게임 for a pro match — use 경기 for real sporting events; 게임 implies casual play.

usage: 휘슬(을) 불다 = 'blow the whistle'; signals a foul or stoppage.
판정(判定) = 'ruling/decision'; 심판 판정 often sparks fan complaints.
A heated shout at a bad call; 똑바로 = 'properly', 봐 is blunt 반말.
오심(誤審) = a refereeing error; a very common sports-news word.
examples: 심판이 우리 팀한테만 불리하게 판정하는 것 같았어요.
It felt like the ref was ruling unfairly against only our team.
한테만 = 'only against'; 불리하게 = 'disadvantageously'.
저 장면은 누가 봐도 오심이에요.
Anyone can see that play was a wrong call.
누가 봐도 = 'no matter who looks / obviously'; 오심 = 'bad call'.
요즘은 비디오 판독으로 심판 오심을 줄여요.
These days they reduce referee errors with video review.
비디오 판독 = 'video review (VAR-style)'; -으로 = 'by means of'.
nuance: 심판 (審判, literally 'examine(審)-judge(判)') is the referee/umpire across all sports, and it doubles as both the official (person) and the act of officiating. To follow sports talk you need its companions: 판정 (判定, 'ruling/decision'), 오심 (誤審, 'erroneous judgment' = a wrong call), and 비디오 판독 (video review), since fans endlessly grumble about 심판 판정. The whistle collocation is 휘슬을 불다. Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, do not say 레퍼리 — the natural word is 심판, the loanword sounds out of place. Second, 심판 has a heavier non-sports sense of divine 'judgment' (최후의 심판 = 'the Last Judgment'); in a sports context it strictly means the on-field official, so context keeps the two apart.
